The bill introduces a new annual charge on all higher education providers registered with TEQSA to recover the costs of its risk monitoring and regulatory oversight activities, with the amount to be set by regulations. The charge will be phased in from 1 January 2022 (20% of costs in 2022, 50% in 2023, 100% in 2024) and is expected to collect around $5.7 million annually, replacing the current partial recovery of about 15% of TEQSA's total costs.

The bills increase TEQSA's cost recovery from about 15% to full cost through higher application fees (from 1 January 2022) and a new annual charge phased in at 20% in 2022, 50% in 2023 and 100% in 2024, originally announced in the 2018–19 budget but delayed due to COVID-19.

The speaker supported the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (Charges) Bill 2021 and the amendment bill, arguing that higher education providers should pay increased cost recovery fees—phased in over three years—to fund TEQSA’s regulatory activities, noting that current cost recovery is about 15% and that the sector had $38 billion in revenue in 2017.

Labor opposes the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (Charges) Bill 2021, arguing that the cost‑recovery measure unfairly burdens a higher education sector already devastated by 17,000 job losses, a 10% real funding cut over three years, soaring student debt of $60,000, and a government‑driven brain drain of researchers.

The speaker supported the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (Charges) Bill 2021 and related amendment, which phase in increased cost recovery for TEQSA from 15% to full cost by 2024, and noted $245 million in federal funding for Edith Cowan University's new Perth campus, set to open in 2025 with $695 million total cost.

The speaker argued for passing the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency cost recovery bills, with fee waivers during COVID and a three-year transition from 2022; they cited $1.5 billion in additional support for public universities, $53 million for private providers, and rebutted opposition claims by stating no public university met JobSeeker eligibility thresholds (30% revenue decline) and that several universities—including Monash ($267M surplus), Melbourne ($178M), Flinders ($35M), USQ ($12M), and Western Sydney ($13M)—reported surpluses in 2020.
Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (Charges) Act 2021
This bill updates the law to introduce a new charge on registered higher education providers, replacing some fees with a broader cost recovery model.
The charge would be set by regulations, with the agency consulting stakeholders on a draft implementation statement before the rules are made.
The charge starts at 20% of costs on 1 January 2022, rises to 50% in 2023, and reaches full cost recovery by 1 January 2024.
The bill requires higher education providers to pay the new charge and any late payment penalties.
Non-payment of the charge would breach a registration condition and could lead to enforcement by the agency.
The bill allows the agency to issue guidelines to help administer the charge.

The bill would make five changes to broadcasting laws to cut red tape and remove outdated rules.
It would cut the annual spending requirement for Australian drama on subscription TV from 10% to 5% and move captioning rules into a ministerial instrument.
The bill would also repeal a clause from the digital radio framework, extend transitional arrangements for ACMA population determinations, and give ACMA more time to award grants until June 2021.
Halve the annual expenditure requirement for Australian drama programming for subscription television broadcasters from 10% to 5%.
Transfer the subscription television captioning rules from the Broadcasting Services Act 1992 to a disallowable ministerial instrument.
Remove a redundant provision from the digital radio framework in the Radiocommunications Act 1992.
Extend grandfathering arrangements for new population determinations by the Australian Communications and Media Authority.
Extend the timeframe for the Australian Communications and Media Authority to implement grants under June 2021.
Subscription television broadcasters, the Australian Communications and Media Authority, and digital radio licensees.

Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021 - Second Reading - Do not reject bill

The majority voted in favour of agreeing with the main idea of the bill. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read it for a [second time](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/). This means that they can now discuss it in more detail. ### What is the bill's main idea? The bill was introduced in order to amend the [Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environment_Protection_and_Biodiversity_Conservation_Act_1999) (EPBC Act) in order to establish: * *a framework for making, varying, revoking and applying National Environmental Standards and* * *an Environment Assurance Commissioner (EAC) to monitor and audit the operation of bilateral agreements with the states and territories as well as to oversee Commonwealth processes under the EPBC Act for making and enforcing approval decisions.* The [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2021a/21bd074) sets out the following 'Key Issues' relating to the bill: * *Industry groups broadly support the Bill, including the framework for National Environmental Standards and the proposed EAC. They consider this Bill, together with the Streamlining Bill, would provide certainty and clarity while addressing regulatory duplication in environmental approvals. However, several industry groups suggest that any National Environmental Standards made under the Bill should reflect the existing requirements of the EPBC Act.* * *Other stakeholders, including environmental, legal and scientific organisations, generally do not support the Bill, expressing considerable concern. Many noted the lack of a comprehensive government response to the Final Report of the Samuel Review, and suggested that the Government was ‘cherry picking’ recommendations and making piecemeal reforms, rather than implementing the full range of ‘tranche 1’ reforms identified in the Final Repor

The majority voted in favour of *disagreeing* with [amendments](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debates/?id=2021-06-23.148.1) introduced by Warringah MP [Zali Steggall](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/warringah/zali_steggall) (Independent), which means they failed. According to MP Steggall, these amendments would "*ensure that measures to safeguard the environment are in place in relation to the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021.*" She explained the purpose of each one in detail in her [contribution to the debate](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debate/?id=2021-06-23.148.2). ### Amendment text > *(1) Schedule 1, item 6, page 5 (line 6), omit "may", substitute "must".* > > *(2) Schedule 1, item 6, page 5 (line 13), omit "may", substitute "must".* > > *(3) Schedule 1, item 6, page 5 (after line 16), after subsection 65C(1), insert:* > >> *(1A) Without limiting subsection (1), the standards made under that subsection must include national standards for each of the following:* >> >>> *(a) matters of national environmental significance;* >>> >>> *(b) transparent processes and robust decisions, including:* >>> >>>> *(i) judicial review; and* >>>> >>>> *(ii) community consultation; and* >>>> >>>> *(iii) adequate assessment of impacts on matters of national environmental significance, including climate impacts; and* >>>> >>> *(iv) emissions profile disclosure; and* >>>> >>>> *(v) regional planning;* >>> >>> *(c) Indigenous engagement and involvement in environmental decision making;* >>> >>> *(d) compliance and enforcement;* >>> >>> *(e) data and information;* >>> >>> *(f) environmental monitoring and evaluation of outcomes;* >>> >>> *(g) environmental restoration, including offsets;* >>> >>> *(h) wildlife permits and trade.* >> >> *(1B) The Minister must take all reasonable steps to ensure that national environmental standards are in force, and comply with subsection (1A), at all times.

The speaker argued that the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021 should be passed to modernise environmental laws through competitive federalism, balancing conservation with economic development, and criticised binary framings of environment versus commerce. He called on the Labor Party to support the bill, referencing Graeme Samuel's review and the need to advance Western Australian projects.

The speaker argued that the government's EPBC Amendment Bill is a rehash of failed 2014 Abbott-era legislation, ignores the Samuel review's recommendations, and fails to provide stronger environmental protections or address delays in project approvals. He moved an amendment noting the government's failure to deliver durable reform and called for a genuine first-stage reform package with stronger standards, independent oversight, and adequate resourcing.

The speaker argued that the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021 should provide greater certainty and consistency in project approvals, citing the New Acland mine’s 14-year delay affecting 350 workers, and noted that all state and territory leaders have agreed to streamline approvals and develop national environmental standards.

Labor opposed the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021, arguing it weakens environmental laws during a biodiversity crisis. The speech cited Auditor-General findings that timely approval decisions dropped from 60% (2014–15) to 5% (2018–19) and 79% of approvals were non‑compliant, and called for stronger protections, a genuinely independent assurance commissioner, and adoption of Professor Graeme Samuel’s review recommendations.

The speaker argued that the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021 would weaken environmental protections by replacing the stronger interim national standards recommended by Professor Graeme Samuel’s independent review with inferior government-drafted standards, allowing the minister to make decisions inconsistent with those standards if deemed in the public interest, and creating an environmental assurance commissioner with no power to investigate individual project decisions—all while Australia already has the world’s highest rate of mammal extinctions and faces escalating climate change impacts.

The EPBC Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021 is inconsistent with the Samuel review and resurrects Tony Abbott's failed one-stop-shop approach. Citing ANAO data showing 95% of decisions are late and 79% noncompliant after 40% funding cuts, the bill was opposed in favour of the full Samuel package, including strong national standards, an independent regulator, and retained Commonwealth intervention powers.

The speaker argued that the bill cements the government's poor environmental record, citing 22 policies in eight years, a divided government, and a lack of firm targets—calling the net-zero 2050 commitment a mere "preference." They highlighted UNESCO's recommendation to list the Great Barrier Reef as endangered, criticised the government's response to Professor Graeme Samuel's review as falling short, and insisted on establishing an independent compliance watchdog with genuine enforcement powers.

The speaker argued the government's bill weakens environmental protections by rejecting expert recommendations, replacing "best available information" with "adequate information," and shifting federal responsibility to states. They opposed the bill, citing the government's poor environmental record, including a 510% increase in job and investment delays and 79% of approvals containing errors.

The bill was opposed as insufficient and contrary to Graeme Samuel's review findings, with the public interest exemption (subclause 65H(7)) allowing circumvention of national standards and the absence of an independent Environment Assurance Commissioner cited as major flaws. Amendments will be moved during consideration in detail to strengthen the standards and require independent expert review.

The speaker opposed the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021, arguing it would weaken environmental protections and hand federal responsibilities to under-resourced states. They cited over 500 community contacts opposing the bill, UNESCO’s draft decision to list the Great Barrier Reef as endangered, and Professor Graeme Samuel’s review calling for fundamental reform with legally enforceable national environmental standards.

The speaker argued that the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021 fails to implement the strong national environmental standards and independent enforcement recommended by the government's own independent review, and that the proposed standards are not scientifically credible according to the Academy of Science. Australia is the world leader in mammal extinction, and the bill will not halt the extinction crisis and may accelerate it.

The speaker argued the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021 is dangerous because it sacrifices environmental protection for political gain, citing the government's failure to act on Graeme Samuel's review recommendations, including implementing national standards and an independent watchdog. The speaker noted that 35% of mammal extinctions since 1500 are Australian, 10 species were listed extinct in March 2021, 79% of EPBC decisions had compliance failures, and assessment times grew by 510%, while the bill does nothing to address these failures.

The speaker argued the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021 would weaken environmental protections, citing hundreds of community emails opposing the legislation, including one from constituent Christine. Concrete points included the government’s devolution of national decision-making to states without implementing Professor Samuel’s full recommendations, and the March 2021 gazettal of 10 species as extinct under the EPBC Act.

Centre Alliance MP Rebekha Sharkie argued the government's EPBC Amendment Bill fails to deliver effective environmental standards, an independent regulator, or a response to the Samuel review, and announced she and Senator Stirling Griff cannot support the bill unless these three conditions are met.

The speaker argued that the government's Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment Bill ignores key recommendations from Professor Graeme Samuel's review, particularly the need for national environmental standards and an independent watchdog. The speaker also criticised the government's record on environmental protection, citing the withdrawal of the live exports bill and the return of Barnaby Joyce as Nationals leader, while promoting Labor's commitment to a complete rewrite of the EPBC Act and highlighting local environmental projects in the electorate of Macnamara.

The bill fails to adopt the robust national environmental standards recommended by the Samuel review, instead allowing the minister to set weak standards without parliamentary oversight for four years and with a public interest exemption to override environmental concerns. The proposed environmental assurance commissioner is also toothless, lacking power to audit individual decisions, compel documents, or operate independently from the minister.

The speaker argued the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021 fails to address the climate and extinction crises, citing a 40% cut to environment department funding, a 510% increase in project delays, and 79% of decisions being noncompliant or erroneous, while criticising the government for ignoring the Samuel review and lacking a genuine net zero commitment.

The speaker supported the EPBC Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021, arguing it implements the Samuel review's 38 recommendations to cut regulatory duplication and project delays, citing costs up to $47 million per month for greenfields projects. The speaker stressed the need for interim national environmental standards, strengthened bilateral frameworks with states, and greater involvement of traditional owners, noting the current system fails both the environment and the economy.

The speaker argued that the government's bill to devolve federal environmental powers to the states is hypocritical, citing previous insistence on Commonwealth control over international relations. They listed specific treaties (World Heritage, Ramsar, IUCN, Bond conventions) and examples of state failures (Great Barrier Reef mining, Franklin dam, Kakadu, Coronation Hill, Murray-Darling Basin Plan), and noted that approval delays stem from public service cuts, not state control—pointing to fast approvals under the last Labor government for projects like Wheatstone, Queensland gas, Prelude, and Olympic Dam.

The government defended the EPBC Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021, arguing it establishes national environmental standards and an environmental assurance commissioner as part of a staged reform process following the Samuel review. It cited over $2 billion in environment spending and a 99 per cent on-time project assessment rate, while accusing Labor of obstruction and inconsistency over support for devolving approvals to the states.

Amendments to the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021 were argued to impose a positive duty on the minister to make National Environmental Standards, remove broad ministerial discretion to exclude decisions from standards, and limit exceptions to national security or emergencies, following recommendations from the Samuel review and the Law Council of Australia.

The speaker argued that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021 is deeply flawed, particularly its stapling provisions that could default three million workers into underperforming funds and its unprecedented directions power giving the Treasurer authority to cancel private sector investments. Labor will move amendments to prevent stapling to underperforming funds and to reject the directions power.

The speaker argued that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021 unfairly targets industry super funds, which have outperformed retail funds (30% asset growth since 2018 versus 3.2%), and that Labor is seeking amendments to protect workers' retirement savings from excessive red tape, regulatory uncertainty, and an ideological attack.

The bill would require employers to check existing super funds via the ATO when a new employee does not nominate one, mandate annual APRA performance tests for funds, and prohibit persistently underperforming funds from accepting new members after two years, with the aim of saving Australians $14 billion over a decade. It also clarifies trustees’ obligations to act solely in members’ financial interests.

The Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021 gives the Treasurer unilateral power to cancel investments, a measure the speaker called illiberal and dangerous, and argued it fails to reduce superannuation fees while potentially locking up to three million Australians into underperforming funds costing $635,000 less in retirement.

The speaker supported schedules 1 and 2 of the bill—which staple super accounts to employees and introduce annual performance testing—but opposed schedule 3, arguing its “best financial interests” covenant, reversal of the burden of proof, and regulation-making power allowing the Treasurer to ban investments could harm members and were not recommended by reviews. They called on the government to rethink schedule 3 and re-engage with stakeholders.

The independent MP announced they will oppose the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021, primarily because schedule 3 gives the Treasurer broad unilateral powers over super fund investments; they support other schedules subject to amendments including delaying stapling until after two years of performance testing and applying the performance test to all funds equally.

The Morrison government's Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021 aims to save Australians $17.9 billion over 10 years by limiting multiple superannuation accounts, requiring annual performance tests for super products, and tightening trustee duties to act in members' best financial interests.

The speaker supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021 for introducing a single default fund, transparency on underperforming funds, and a best-interest duty, and argued Labor opposed it to protect union funding and influence.

The speaker opposed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021, arguing it would allow workers to be stapled to underperforming superannuation funds, replace trustees’ duty to act in members’ best interests with a narrower “best financial interests” standard that could discourage long-term community investments, and give the Treasurer excessive power via unfinished regulations—reflecting what the speaker described as a government ideological attack on industry superannuation, despite industry funds outperforming retail funds and the royal commission finding widespread abuse in retail funds only.

The speaker gave qualified support for the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021, urging amendments such as sequencing to eliminate poor-performing funds before the stapling provision begins, extending annual performance tests to all superannuation products not just MySuper, and setting a financial threshold on best‑financial‑interest provisions to avoid unnecessary administrative costs. They welcomed the removal of the directions power and specifically opposed the use of compulsory superannuation for political donations, advertising at sporting events, or corporate box hire.

The Morrison government's Your Future, Your Super Bill implements Productivity Commission and banking royal commission recommendations to prevent multiple super accounts, empower member choice, penalise underperforming funds, and increase transparency, projected to save Australians nearly $18 billion over 10 years.

Social Security Legislation Amendment (Remote Engagement Program) Bill 2021

Introduced the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Remote Engagement Program) Bill 2021, which creates a pilot program for a new supplementary payment to eligible jobseekers in remote communities who volunteer for at least 15 hours per week in skill-building placements, aiming to address the decline in Indigenous employment from 54% to 49% between 2007-08 and 2018-19. The pilot will replace the Community Development Program (CDP) in 2023 and is part of the National Agreement on Closing the Gap.

The speaker argued that the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Remote Engagement Program) Bill 2021 addresses the lack of employment opportunities in remote Australia, citing research that work improves health, wellbeing, and reduces poverty and social exclusion. They noted that less than two per cent of actively trading businesses are located in remote areas, which disproportionately affects Indigenous Australians.

The speaker argued that the Security Legislation Amendment (Critical Infrastructure) Bill 2020 is necessary to protect Australia's critical infrastructure from increasing cyberattacks and grey zone activities, citing specific attacks on hospitals, a food wholesaler, and a water provider. The bill mandates risk-management programs, cybersecurity incident reporting to the Australian Signals Directorate, and includes last-resort government intervention powers.
Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment (High Risk Terrorist Offenders) Bill 2021

The Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment (High Risk Terrorist Offenders) Bill 2020 creates extended supervision orders for high-risk terrorist offenders after their custodial sentences, citing the 2019 London Bridge and 2020 Streatham attacks, and the government accepted 10 of 11 recommendations from the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security.
Surveillance Legislation Amendment (Identify and Disrupt) Bill 2021

The speaker argued in support of the Surveillance Legislation Amendment (Identify and Disrupt) Bill 2020, which introduces network activity, data disruption and account takeover warrants to combat online crime on the dark web, citing a 163% increase in child abuse material and 696 search warrants, 290 charges and 139 weapons seized via Operation Ironside. The speaker also noted that 39% of federally convicted child-sex offenders previously spent no time in jail.
Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment (Sunsetting Review and Other Measures) Bill 2021

The speaker argued for the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment (Sunsetting Review and Other Measures) Bill 2021, which extends declared areas provisions to 2024, control orders and preventative detention orders to December 2022, and emergency stop, search and seizure powers to December 2022. They cited a "probable" national terrorism threat level, noting 136 people charged in 64 counter-terrorism operations since 2014, nine attacks, and around 230 Australians having travelled to Syria or Iraq to support extremist groups.
Customs Amendment (2022 Harmonized System Changes) Bill 2021

The Customs Amendment (2022 Harmonized System Changes) Bill 2021 updates Australia’s tariff codes to align with the international 2022 Harmonized System, creating new classifications for edible insects, drones, 3D printers, e-waste, and e-cigarettes, with duty rates set to free for flat panel displays, semiconductor based transducers, and electronic waste to avoid harming importers. The Morrison government aims to keep pace with changing trade patterns and support trade diversification, notably after Chinese tariffs hit Australian wine and rock lobster industries.
Customs Tariff Amendment (Incorporation of Proposals) Bill 2021

The Customs Tariff Amendment (Incorporation of Proposals) Bill 2021 extends tariff exemptions for PPE imports ($3.8 million), F-35 Joint Strike Fighter components ($6.7 million), and low-emission vehicle R&D ($1.7 million), while noting 13.6 million COVID-19 vaccine doses administered and 22% of Australians fully vaccinated.
